title: Module 12 Interpretation Check
intro: Each item gives you a short research situation. Decide what the evidence supports.

items.q: A university finds r = .10 between SAT scores and first year GPA among admitted students, but the national r is higher. What is the most likely reason?
o: Range restriction. Admitted students have a narrow range of SAT scores
items.why: Admission removes low scorers, so the data do not cover the full range of SAT scores.

items.q: A scatterplot shows a clear arch. Pearson r is near 0. What is the right conclusion?
o: The variables are strongly related in a curved way that r cannot capture
items.why: Pearson r is blind to nonlinear patterns.

items.q: A researcher reports r = .85 for 30 points, but one point is far from the rest. What should be done first?
o: Examine the scatterplot and check how r changes with the outlier removed
Remove the point without saying so
items.why: Report both analyses and justify any exclusion. One point should not decide the conclusion.

items.q: Two reliable measures correlate at r = .50. A third measure with poor reliability correlates with the first at r = .15. What is a plausible explanation?
o: Measurement error in the third measure weakens the observed correlation
The sample size was too small for any correlation
items.why: Low reliability caps the correlation you can observe.

items.q: Hospital A's patients show r = .40 between age and days in the hospital, and Hospital B's patients also show r = .40. When the data from both hospitals are pooled, r = .15. What explains this?
o: Group differences on the variables can change a pooled correlation
A computational error must have occurred
items.why: The pooled r reflects the relation within groups plus the offset between groups.
